274.title: The saint-soldier
274.hook: the Khalsa ideal holds prayer and courage together in one person
274.tomorrow: Two flags at the Akal Takht
274.howItsDone: Sikhs describe the Khalsa ideal as sant sipahi, saint-soldier: an initiated Sikh keeps the daily prayers and discipline and also stands ready to defend the weak and resist injustice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rehat Maryada, and your line, a shared code. That closed our days on the Sikh way of life. Today a new stretch begins: sword and saint. Day two hundred seventy-four.

Picture two people. One sits cross-legged at dawn, eyes closed, lips moving with a prayer. The other stands between a bully and the kid being bullied, and doesn't step aside. Most of us file them in different drawers. The quiet one and the brave one. The monk and the firefighter. The Sikh tradition keeps asking a stubborn question: why not the same person? Why not someone who prays at dawn and, when it's needed, stands in the doorway? Today: the saint-soldier.
screen: `ONE PRAYS AT DAWN.` → `ONE STANDS IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHY NOT THE SAME PERSON?`

segments.voice: Sant is a saint, a holy person, someone whose mind rests in God. Sipahi is a soldier. It's a Persian word, and the English word sepoy comes from it. Put them together, sant sipahi, and you have one of the best-known ways Sikhs describe the Khalsa ideal. The idea has a history. The first Gurus were teachers of the Name, poets and farmers. Then, in 1606, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, was executed in Lahore by the Mughal authorities. His son, Guru Hargobind, became the sixth Guru as a boy, and tradition says he put on two swords. One he called miri, worldly responsibility. The other he called piri, spiritual authority. Both, worn at once. Nearly a century later, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and gave the idea its fullest form. The Khalsa would keep the daily prayers and the discipline of the Name, and also stand ready to protect the weak and resist injustice. Notice the order. The saint comes first in the phrase, and in the life. The daily prayers aren't a warm-up before the real work. They're the root, and courage grows out of them. Without the saint, the soldier is only force. Without the soldier, the saint may watch injustice and do nothing. Sikhs don't read this as a call to go looking for fights. Most saint-soldiers never touch a weapon beyond the small kirpan. Their courage looks like telling the truth in a meeting, or refusing to laugh along. The prayer steadies them. The courage makes it real.
screen: `SANT — SAINT. SIPAHI — SOLDIER.` · `1606: TWO SWORDS, MIRI AND PIRI.` · `1699: THE KHALSA HOLDS BOTH.` · `THE SAINT COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `SAINT AND SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Two halves, then. First, the saint. Sit still and settle. If you pray, you can use a line you know. If not, just rest your mind on something good and true for a few breaths. Then, the soldier. Bring to mind one small brave thing waiting for you today: a hard conversation, a truth to tell, someone to stand beside. Don't do it yet. Just decide you will, from this steady place. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sant sipahi. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage held together in one person, with the saint first.
Your line: saint and soldier. Today, pray or pause first, then do the one brave thing you decided on. Day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: Two flags at the Akal Takht
275.word: Two flags at the Akal Takht
275.hook: two Nishan Sahibs stand there, for worldly and spiritual sovereignty, the spiritual one slightly higher
275.howItsDone: Every gurdwara flies a Nishan Sahib, a saffron flag bearing the khanda; at the Akal Takht in Amritsar two stand side by side for miri and piri, and Sikhs bow toward the Akal Takht as the highest seat of Sikh authority.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant sipahi, the saint-soldier. Your line was saint and soldier, and we met Guru Hargobind's two swords. Today, those two swords become two flags. Day two hundred seventy-five.

Drive through almost any town with Sikhs in it, from Punjab to Surrey to Yuba City, and look up. Somewhere above the rooftops there's a tall pole wrapped in saffron cloth, with a triangular saffron flag at the top. That's how you find the gurdwara. That flag is the Nishan Sahib, and every gurdwara flies one. But in Amritsar, at the Akal Takht, facing the Golden Temple, there are two. Side by side. And if you look closely, they aren't quite the same height. Today: two flags at the Akal Takht.
screen: `A SAFFRON FLAG ABOVE THE ROOFTOPS.` → `EVERY GURDWARA HAS ONE.` → `AT THE AKAL TAKHT, TWO.`

segments.voice: Nishan means a sign, a mark. Sahib is a word of honor. So the Nishan Sahib is the honored sign, the flag that says: here is a gurdwara, here you can find shelter and food. It carries the khanda, the Sikh emblem. Now the Akal Takht. Akal means timeless, beyond death: one of the oldest names Sikhs use for God. Takht means throne. Guru Hargobind raised it in 1606, the same years he took up the two swords, right across from the Harmandir. The Harmandir was the place of prayer. The Takht would be the place where the community's worldly affairs were heard and decided. It's still the highest seat of Sikh authority. Between the Akal Takht and the Harmandir stand the two Nishan Sahibs. Sikhs call them by the names of Guru Hargobind's swords. One is miri, worldly sovereignty: responsibility for justice, for the community, for the world as it is. The other is piri, spiritual sovereignty: the Name, prayer, the life of the soul. And the piri flag stands slightly higher. That's the whole lesson, written in the sky. The Sikh tradition doesn't ask its people to pick between the world and the spirit. It raises both. But it doesn't pretend they're equal either. Worldly power is meant to answer to the spiritual. Courage is meant to serve prayer, not the other way round. Two poles, a short walk apart, and the difference in height is small enough to miss. That's fitting too. The spirit doesn't have to tower. It just has to be a little higher.
screen: `NISHAN SAHIB — THE HONORED SIGN.` · `AKAL TAKHT — THE TIMELESS THRONE.` · `MIRI AND PIRI, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE PIRI FLAG STANDS SLIGHTLY HIGHER.` · then, large: `SPIRIT A LITTLE HIGHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up. Feet under your hips. Let your spine grow tall, like a flagpole, the crown of your head lifting just a little higher than it was. Stay there for a minute, breathing easily. Feel how the body holds you up without strain. Then sit, and keep that little lift. Ask yourself: in my day today, what's the higher flag? Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Two flags at the Akal Takht. The miri flag for worldly sovereignty, the piri flag for spiritual sovereignty, and the spiritual one a little higher.
screen: `TWO FLAGS AT THE AKAL TAKHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: spirit a little higher. Today, when a practical choice pulls at you, ask which answer keeps the spirit a little higher. Day two hundred seventy-five.

276.title: The kirpan, explained
276.hook: the word is often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor
276.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan at all times as one of the five Ks, usually small and sheathed on a cloth strap called a gatra; many explain it as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor, and a duty to protect others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two flags at the Akal Takht, and your line, spirit a little higher. Today, the small sword every initiated Sikh wears, and what its name is said to hold. Day two hundred seventy-six.

Airports, schools, courtrooms. For decades, the kirpan has made headlines when a security guard spots it: a small curved blade in a sheath, worn on a cloth strap under a Sikh's clothes. The headlines usually ask one question. Is it a weapon? A few days ago we met the kirpan as one of the five Ks. Today we slow down on something the headlines skip. Before anyone argues about what it is, listen to what its name is often said to mean. Today: the kirpan, explained.
screen: `AIRPORTS, SCHOOLS, COURTROOMS.` → `IS IT A WEAPON?` → `FIRST, LISTEN TO THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Sikh teachers often explain the word kirpan by splitting it in two. Kirpa: grace, mercy, kindness. The same word appears in the Guru Granth Sahib again and again for God's grace, the gift nobody earns. And aan: honor, dignity, self-respect. Kirpa plus aan. Mercy and honor. Here's the honest part. Language scholars trace kirpan to an older Sanskrit word, kripana, which simply means a sword or a knife. So the mercy-and-honor reading is best understood as a teaching explanation, the way a preacher might unpack a word, rather than its original root. But notice which part comes first in the explanation. Kirpa. Mercy leads. Honor follows. The kirpan is worn as a reminder of a duty: to protect the weak, to stand for justice, to guard the dignity of others as well as your own. It's never meant for anger or for show. The Sikh code of conduct lists it among the five Ks without which an initiated Sikh is not fully dressed. Many Sikhs wear a small one, some only a few inches long, and they will tell you that the moment it's drawn in temper, its meaning is lost. So the kirpan carries its own warning. A blade that is mostly mercy. That's why, when courts in several countries have looked closely, many have accepted it as a religious article with safeguards, rather than a weapon. And that's why Sikhs say its real work happens in the sheath. It's a reminder that you're responsible for the people around you, and that mercy comes first.
screen: `KIRPA — GRACE, MERCY.` · `AAN — HONOR, DIGNITY.` · `THE ROOT: SANSKRIT KRIPANA, A BLADE.` · `MERCY LEADS, HONOR FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `MERCY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're a little annoyed with right now. Someone who owes you an apology, or who got something wrong. Picture them clearly. Now, instead of rehearsing what you'd say, ask what mercy would look like here. Not pretending it didn't matter: that would cost your honor. Just a little grace, offered first. Maybe a softer message, maybe letting one thing go. Choose one merciful act you could do today. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The kirpan. The small sword of an initiated Sikh, often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor. Mercy comes first.
Your line: mercy first. Today, do the merciful thing you chose, before you decide whether you were right. Day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: When the sword is right
277.hook: the Zafarnama says that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword (Zafarnama 22)
277.howItsDone: Sikhs cite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to Aurangzeb, for the principle that force is justified only as a last resort, after every other means has failed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kirpan: kirpa and aan, mercy and honor. Your line was mercy first. Did you offer one small grace? Today, the hardest question about any sword: when, if ever, is it right? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Picture a man who has lost almost everything in a single winter. His city has been besieged for months. His enemies swore solemn oaths, on their holiest things, that he and his people could leave in safety. They broke those oaths the moment he stepped outside. In the weeks that followed, all four of his sons were killed. And then he sits down and writes a letter to the most powerful man on earth, the emperor behind it all. Today: when the sword is right.
screen: `A CITY BESIEGED.` → `SOLEMN OATHS, BROKEN.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: The man is Guru Gobind Singh. The winter is 1704 into 1705. After the siege of Anandpur and the broken oaths, his two elder sons died fighting at Chamkaur. His two youngest, still small boys, were executed at Sirhind. Tradition says the Guru wrote the letter soon after, in Persian verse, the language of the Mughal court, and sent it to the emperor Aurangzeb. It's called the Zafarnama, the letter of victory. A strange title for a letter written after so much loss. But the victory it claims isn't on a battlefield. It's moral. The letter doesn't beg, and it doesn't rage. It calmly reminds the emperor of the oaths his men swore, and says that a ruler who breaks his word has lost something no army can win back. And in one couplet, number twenty-two in the usual numbering, it sets out a principle. In plain words: when every other means has been tried and has failed, it is right to take hold of the sword. Read that slowly and notice where the weight falls. Not on the sword. On everything that comes before it. Talking. Petition. Patience. Agreements. Every other means. The sword is not the first answer. It's the last one, and only when the others are truly used up. That's the line Sikhs point to when people ask how a tradition of prayer can carry a blade. Force isn't forbidden. But it has to earn its place, by coming last. Most days, of course, the question never reaches the sword. It stops at the next conversation, the next try.
screen: `ANANDPUR, THEN CHAMKAUR AND SIRHIND.` · `ZAFARNAMA — THE LETTER OF VICTORY.` · `THE VICTORY IS MORAL, NOT MILITARY.` · `ONLY WHEN EVERY OTHER MEANS HAS FAILED.` · then, large: `EVERY OTHER MEANS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of a conflict in your life that's stuck. Maybe you've already decided to fight it out, go cold, or give up. Before you do, list the other means in your head. Have you asked plainly? Listened fully? Put it in writing? Asked someone to help? Waited a day? Find one peaceful way you haven't really tried yet. Just one. Picture yourself trying it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
When the sword is right. The Zafarnama's principle: only when every other means has been tried and has failed.
screen: `WHEN THE SWORD IS RIGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every other means first. Today, try the one peaceful way you haven't tried yet, before anything harder. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: Rules of a righteous fight
278.hook: tradition holds that a just fight never harms the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent
278.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of dharam yudh, a righteous fight taken up only in defense of justice, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded of both sides, as its example; many Sikh relief groups today name their work after this ideal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the sword is right: only when every other means has failed. Your line was every other means first. Today, the next question. If a fight does come, how must it be fought? Day two hundred seventy-eight.
screen: `WHEN THE SWORD IS RIGHT — EVERY OTHER MEANS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Anyone who has had a sibling knows there are rules even in a fight. No hitting below the belt. Leave the little one out of it. When somebody says stop, you stop. Break those and the fight turns into something uglier, and everyone can feel it. Armies have always needed the same kind of rules, and most of history is the story of armies ignoring them. The Sikh tradition has a name for a fight that keeps its rules. Today: dharam yudh.
screen: `EVEN SIBLINGS HAVE RULES.` → `BREAK THEM, AND IT TURNS UGLY.` → `A FIGHT THAT KEEPS ITS RULES.`

segments.voice: Dharam is duty, righteousness, the right order of things. Yudh is war, battle. Dharam yudh: a righteous fight. Not a fight for land, loot or revenge, but one taken up, as a last resort, in defense of what is right. Sikh tradition holds that such a fight has limits. You don't strike the unarmed. You don't pursue someone who's running away. You don't harm those who surrender, or women and children, or anyone who isn't fighting. You don't plunder homes or desecrate places of worship. The sources for these rules are mostly tradition and the old Sikh histories, rather than one list in scripture, and historians will tell you not every battle lived up to them. But the ideal is clear, and there's one story Sikhs tell to show it. During the battles around Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya went across the battlefield carrying a water skin. He gave water to the wounded. All the wounded, including the soldiers fighting against the Sikhs. Some Sikhs were furious, and brought him to Guru Gobind Singh. Why are you helping the enemy? Tradition says Bhai Ghanaiya answered that he didn't see friend or enemy on that field. In every face he saw the Guru. The Guru didn't scold him. He gave him ointment, and told him to dress their wounds as well. Many Sikhs today remember Bhai Ghanaiya as a forerunner of humanitarian aid. And that's the heart of dharam yudh. Even in the middle of a fight, the other person never stops being a person.
screen: `DHARAM — RIGHT. YUDH — FIGHT.` · `NEVER THE UNARMED, FLEEING OR INNOCENT.` · `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` · `THE ENEMY IS STILL A PERSON.` · then, large: `FAIR, EVEN IN CONFLICT.`

segments.voice: Think of a disagreement you're in right now, big or small. At work, at home, online. Picture the other person, not as a position, but as a face. Now check your own rules of the fight. Am I being fair to what they actually said? Am I hitting where they can't defend? Am I dragging in someone who isn't part of it? Pick one rule you'll keep, even if they don't. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dharam yudh. A righteous fight: taken up only for what's right, and never against the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent.
Your line: fair, even in conflict. Today, in one disagreement, keep the rule you picked, whatever the other side does. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

279.title: Gatka, the moving prayer
279.hook: the Sikh martial art, practiced with sticks and swords, often as a moving meditation
279.howItsDone: Gatka is taught in many gurdwaras and Sikh youth groups; teams perform it at nagar kirtan processions and at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, and many practitioners keep Waheguru in mind as they move.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharam yudh, the righteous fight with rules. Your line was fair, even in conflict. Did you keep your rule in one disagreement? Today, where those old skills live now: in a dance. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

If you've ever watched a Sikh procession on a festival day, you might have seen this. The road is cleared in a wide circle. A drum starts. Two young people step into the space with wooden sticks and small round shields, and they begin to circle each other, feet light, sticks flashing, the crowd shouting. It looks like a fight. Then you notice their faces. Calm. Focused. Almost peaceful. And sometimes their lips are moving. Today: gatka, the moving prayer.
screen: `A CLEARED CIRCLE, A DRUM.` → `STICKS FLASHING, FEET LIGHT.` → `CALM FACES, MOVING LIPS.`

segments.voice: Gatka is the Sikh martial art. In its best-known form today, it's practiced with a wooden stick, the soti, and a small shield, the phari. Some practitioners also train with swords, spears and other traditional weapons. It grew out of older fighting arts that the Sikhs of the Gurus' time trained in, when the Khalsa had to defend itself. Where the word gatka itself comes from, sources disagree, and nobody can say for sure. Today gatka appears at nagar kirtans, the processions that carry the Guru Granth Sahib through the streets, and especially at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, the spring festival of martial skill that tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh. There are also gatka competitions and teams, with rules, points and safety gear. But the heart of it, for many Sikhs, isn't scoring. Gatka rests on footwork, a pattern of steps called the paintra. You learn to move with balance and rhythm before you ever swing a stick. And many teachers say the movement should be done in remembrance: with Waheguru in the breath, the Name kept in mind while the body moves. That's why people call it a moving prayer. It's the saint-soldier in one practice. The body is trained, strong and quick. The mind is kept still and remembering. And the point isn't to hurt anyone. It's to be ready, and steady, at the same time. A mind that stays calm while the sticks are flying is a mind that can stay calm in a hard meeting, too.
screen: `SOTI AND PHARI — STICK AND SHIELD.` · `NAGAR KIRTAN AND HOLA MOHALLA.` · `PAINTRA — FOOTWORK FIRST.` · `THE BODY MOVES, THE MIND REMEMBERS.` · then, large: `MOVE WITH PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand. Shift your weight slowly onto your right foot, then your left, then back. Let your arms swing a little, loose and easy, as if you were holding a light stick. Keep your breath slow. With each step, give the mind one word to rest on: a word you pray with, if you pray, or simply now. Move like that for a minute, then come to stillness and sit. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Gatka. The Sikh martial art of stick, shield and sword, practiced by many as a moving meditation: the body quick, the mind remembering.
Your line: move with prayer. Today, on one walk, climb or chore, keep a single word in the breath while your body moves. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

280.title: The Nihangs
280.hook: blue-robed Sikh orders who keep the old martial traditions alive
280.howItsDone: Nihang orders live communally in camps called chhaunis, wear blue with the tall dumalla turban, keep horses and traditional weapons, and gather in great numbers at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur each spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gatka, the moving prayer. Your line was move with prayer. Did one walk or chore get a word in the breath? Today, the people who never stopped living the old martial ways. Day two hundred eighty.

Anandpur, in spring, at Hola Mohalla. Out of the dust come riders on horseback, standing in the stirrups at a gallop, spears raised. They wear deep blue robes. Their turbans are enormous, stacked high, and ringed with small steel circles and emblems that flash in the sun. It looks like a scene from three hundred years ago, and in a way it is. These are the Nihangs. Today we meet them, and then look back on a week of sword and saint.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN SPRING.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.` → `TURBANS RINGED WITH STEEL.`

segments.voice: The Nihangs are orders of Sikh warriors who keep the Khalsa's old martial life going. They're sometimes called Akali Nihangs, from Akal, the Timeless: the ones who belong to the Timeless. They wear blue, a color tradition links to Guru Gobind Singh. They tie the tall turban called a dumalla, often carrying small steel weapons and quoits, the chakkar, in its folds. They keep horses, train with traditional weapons, and many live a traveling, communal life in their camps, called chhaunis. In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa was fighting to survive, Nihang bands were among its fiercest defenders. Where the name comes from, sources give different answers. Some explain it from a Persian word for a crocodile, a creature fearless in the water. Others from roots meaning without fear, or without attachment. Nobody can settle it, and each explanation says something Nihangs value. Not every Sikh lives like a Nihang, and the Nihangs are a small part of the panth. But at Hola Mohalla, the spring gathering tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur, it's the Nihangs' riding and mock battles that much of the crowd comes to see. Now look back at this week. The saint-soldier, prayer and courage in one person. Two flags, the spirit a little higher. The kirpan, mercy first. When the sword is right: every other means first. Dharam yudh: fair, even in conflict. Gatka: move with prayer. And the Nihangs: the old ways kept. Tomorrow, the last day of this stretch, and the fight the Gurus cared about most.
screen: `AKALI NIHANGS — THOSE OF THE TIMELESS.` · `BLUE ROBES, TALL DUMALLA, HORSES.` · `A NAME WITH MANY EXPLANATIONS.` · `A WEEK OF SWORD AND SAINT.` · then, large: `THE OLD WAYS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who keeps an old way alive. A grandparent who still cooks the family dish from memory. A neighbor who mends instead of throwing away. A friend who still writes letters by hand. Picture them doing it. Notice the patience in it, and what would be lost if nobody did. If you like, choose one old way of your own you'd like to keep going. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
